criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design. Discusses context of ethical issues in engineering organisations. Identifies the relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Introduction identifies the central ethical issues (public safety vs business pressure, professional integrity), situates them in engineering organisations, and explicitly lists stakeholders. However, only one core dilemma is developed rather than several distinct issues with their significance, so not Excellent.

evidence.quote: The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel's company, the chip contract company, the government health department
the issue of maintaining product quality safety while trying to succeed as a business in a competitive field

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions of the ethical issues. Draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Balanced for/against arguments with reasonable depth (competitive advantage, revenue, future QA capability vs harm, integrity, reputation), leading to a clear conclusion. Decision-making recommendations focus on Rachel and her company; other stakeholders (health department, end-users) are not given decision guidance.

evidence.where: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship
evidence.quote: shipping the servers on time would give Rachel's company a competitive advantage in the market
the short-term benefit trade-off is greatly outweighed by the potential risks of harm to end-users

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument, which justifies the conclusion. The body of the report follows a logical structure, with paragraphs linked and content ordered in a way that is easy to follow and support the building of the argument. Arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Report follows a logical for/against structure building to the conclusion, which is well supported by the harm case study, code of ethics and reputation arguments. Understanding is sound, though the 'grow now to fix QA later' argument is underdeveloped and not fully resolved.

evidence.quote: By refusing to ship, Rachel would demonstrate her professional integrity and commitment to public safety
the decision to Not Ship is certainly the most ethical path

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence. Research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Four references including two external case studies (NHS IT failures, VW emissions), the EA Code of Ethics, and some quantitative evidence (deaths, fines, lost letters). Understanding is good, but the CNBC Apple-marketing source is tangential and not every argument is case-study supported.

evidence.quote: several hundred thousand hospital letters being lost
billions of dollars in fines and legal fees

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections which serve their respective functions well: abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion. Maps, figures, tables, and any visual elements are correctly used to support written discussions. The writing is free from any grammatical errors. The expression is fluent, has appropriate word choice, is concise, easy to read and understand. References are well-structured and appropriate providing strong support of the motivations in the report.
criteria.reasoning: Correct report sections (abstract, introduction, body, conclusion, IEEE-style references), but no figures, tables or any visual elements. Several language errors: 'DICUSSION', repeated misuse of 'EACE' for the EA Code, 'benefits of could', 'have her company might go under'. Fluent overall, so Good is the best fit.

overall: A well-structured, balanced ethics report with a clearly justified 'Not Ship' recommendation supported by the EA Code and two strong external case studies. Weakened by limited stakeholder-specific decision guidance, thin sourcing for some arguments, no visual elements, and several language/abbreviation errors.

feedback.summary: Your report is well structured and reaches a clearly justified 'Not Ship' recommendation, supported by the EA Code of Ethics and two strong case studies (NHS, VW). Your introduction identifies the core dilemma and stakeholders, and your for/against discussion is balanced. To reach the top band, develop several distinct ethical issues, give decision guidance to all stakeholders, strengthen evidence for weaker arguments, and add visual elements while fixing language errors.
next_steps: Add a stakeholder-by-stakeholder decision-making discussion (health department, end-users, chip contractor), not just Rachel and her company, to lift C2 to Excellent.

Support the 'ship now to fund future QA' argument in 'The Most Ethical Path' with evidence or a case study, or remove/reframe it, and state an explicit criterion for when shipping with known defects could be acceptable.

Add visual elements (e.g. a stakeholder-interests table, decision matrix or risk-benefit figure), correct 'DICUSSION' and 'EACE' to 'EA', fix grammatical errors, and complete reference [3] with a URL.

criteria.C1: Your introduction clearly identifies the central dilemma (public safety vs business pressure) and lists stakeholders, including Rachel, her company, the chip contractor and the health department. To reach Excellent, develop several distinct ethical issues with their significance — e.g. professional integrity, reputational risk, and end-user safety as separate issues — rather than one core dilemma.
criteria.C2: Your for/against arguments (competitive advantage and revenue vs harm, integrity and reputation) show reasonable depth and lead to a clear conclusion. The next level requires decision-making recommendations for several different stakeholders — currently your guidance focuses on Rachel and her company, with little for the health department or end-users.
criteria.C3: Your report follows a logical for/against structure that builds well to the 'Not Ship' conclusion, supported by the harm case study, the EA Code and reputation arguments. To reach Excellent, fully resolve the 'grow now to fix QA later' argument in 'The Most Ethical Path' so every strand of the argument supports the conclusion systematically.
criteria.C4: Your four references, including the NHS IT failures and VW emissions case studies with quantitative evidence (lost letters, fines), substantiate key arguments well. For Excellent, ensure every argument is evidenced — the future-QA-improvement claim currently has no support — and replace the tangential Apple marketing source with one directly relevant to competitive advantage.
criteria.C5: Your report has all required sections and IEEE-style references, and reads fluently overall. However, it contains no figures, tables or visual elements, and has language errors: 'DICUSSION', repeated use of 'EACE' instead of EA, 'benefits of could very well', and 'have her company might go under'. Fixing these and adding visuals would lift you to Very good or Excellent.
